text: `new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass()` is true. Why?
choices: Both lists are empty, so the JVM shares a single instance until an element is added.
Type arguments are erased after compilation — both are `java.util.ArrayList` holding `Object` references at run time.
`getClass()` returns the raw type by design, though the parameterized types differ underneath.
The two type arguments happen to erase to the same bound; `List<int[]>` would differ.
explanation: There is no class `ArrayList<String>` at run time. The compiler checks the type argument and inserts casts, then removes it entirely — what runs is what Java 1.4 had. So generics are a compile-time discipline over an untyped runtime, and the guarantee is conditional: if your code compiled without unchecked warnings, the inserted casts will never fail.
